notes.body:
The golden chain — سلسلۃ الذھب — is the unbroken line of transmission running through the Imams, one handing to the next, reaching back to the Prophet and through him to the source of revelation. It is called golden not for beauty but for purity: every link is an inheritor of divine knowledge, so nothing false can pass along it. What travels down it is not rumor but light carried from one trusted keeper to another.

The most treasured word borne on that chain is the declaration of oneness itself. In the celebrated report the kalima — لا الہ الا اللہ — is named the fortress of Allah, and whoever enters it is kept safe; yet the report adds that the Imam is himself among the conditions of that fortress. **The testimony of oneness and the guardian of that testimony arrive together, on the same chain.**

Placed beside the chain, the sermon that opens نھج البلاغہ changes in weight. Maulana Ali (ع) is not one thinker among many venturing an opinion about Allah; he is a link in that golden chain and the very condition of the kalima, now unfolding what the kalima means. His words on oneness are not speculation reaching upward — they are transmission flowing down.

The sermon even enacts the chain's own logic, for the testimony moves in two motions and the sermon lives inside both:

- the negation, نفی — لا الہ, "no deity" — stripping away every limit the mind would fix upon Allah;
- the affirmation, اثبات — الا اللہ, "except Allah" — letting only the Real remain.

Read alone, the sermon is a breathtaking meditation on a truth beyond words. Read as the utterance of one who is himself a condition of the kalima, it becomes the fortress explained from the inside by its own keeper — the golden chain speaking of the very oneness it was forged to carry. That is why it reaches full weight only once the chain is held in view.
notes.anchor: With that golden chain in view
notes.quote: With that golden chain in view
etymology: خطبۃ (sermon): from the root خ-ط-ب, seen in خِطاب (an address) and خاطَبَ (to address someone). Built on the measure فُعْلَۃ carrying a passive sense — a thing recited — it names the formal address a خطیب delivers from the pulpit: an exhortation spoken aloud to a gathering, which is exactly what Maulana Ali proclaims here.

سلسلۃ (chain): from the root س-ل-س-ل, whose very doubling — the same sounds looping back on themselves — pictures link fastened to link. The word names anything joined in unbroken succession; here it is the succession of Imams, each one bound to the last so that no gap lets falsehood slip in.

نفی (negation): from the root ن-ف-ي, which also carries the sense of banishing or driving into exile. To negate is to drive a false notion out — so لا الہ banishes every limited idea the mind would set up in place of the Real, clearing the ground before the affirmation can stand.

اثبات (affirmation): from the root ث-ب-ت, to be firm, fixed, and standing fast. Its form-IV sense is to make a thing stand firm — so الا اللہ adds no new idea but lets the one enduring Reality remain fixed in place once all else has been swept away.

notes.body:
Every attribute is a description we lay onto something — and a description, by its very nature, is not the thing it describes. Whiteness is not the wall it colours; strength is not the arm that carries it. So the moment we say Allah *has* an attribute, we have quietly set beside Him something that is not Him.

That "setting beside" is the whole engine of the chain. **To hang a quality on Allah is to place a second reality next to His** — the essence on one side, the attribute on the other — and a second reality standing next to Him is what it means to give Him a companion, even when we only meant to praise Him.

Follow where that leads, one step drawing on the next:

1. We assign an attribute — a "second" that is other than Him.
2. That second is joined to Him, so He now has a companion.
3. A companion makes a pair — He is counted as "two."
4. A pair is a composite — He is broken into parts.
5. Whatever is made of parts leans on those parts to exist, and to lean is to be needy — the mark of a creature, never the Creator.

This is why the perfection of sincerity (اخلاص) is the stripping-away of attributes (نفی الصفۃ). We do not deny that Allah is merciful or mighty; **we deny only that His mercy is a thing standing beside Him.** Each name is affirmed as nothing but Allah Himself — لا الہ erasing the small picture our minds draw, الا اللہ affirming the boundless Reality no picture can hold.
notes.anchor: whoever makes Him two has broken Him into parts
notes.quote: whoever makes Him two has broken Him into parts
etymology: صفة (attribute): from the root و-ص-ف, to describe or depict. A صفة never stands alone in the language — it always trails a described noun (موصوف), so the word itself carries the very problem the sermon exposes: an attribute is a second thing that points back to something other than itself.

قرن (joining): from the root ق-ر-ن, to couple or yoke together. A قرین is a companion or consort, and a قرن is the horn set as one of a matched pair on a head — the root pictures two things bound side by side, which is precisely what an attribute does to Allah.

ثنی (making two): from the root ث-ن-ي, to double or to fold back; اثنان means "two." To fold is to lay one layer against another, so to count Allah as "two" is to fold a second reality onto the One who cannot be reckoned among numbers.

جزء (part): from the root ج-ز-أ, to divide or portion out. A جزء is a piece cut from a whole, and whatever is cut into pieces depends on those pieces to be whole again — dependence being the mark of a creature, never the self-sufficient Creator.
